And every one of those mornings started the same way, a wooden kitchen

She lived in a small town north of Sendai, in a wooden house with a narrow garden
and a screen door that stuck in the summer. She lived to 98 and
she walked every one of those days. When she was 90,
she could still walk to the fish shop and back without stopping.
People in the town knew her walk. Small steps, one hand on her hip, one
hand with the shopping bag. She never ran, she never hurried,
she just went. I taught physical education for 32 years,
boys and girls, middle school, on a schoolyard with more dust than grass.
I taught them volleyball, running, jump rope,
and I taught them to stretch before the bell. And after I retired, I taught the neighbour women
in their 70s how to do these same movements while sitting on a chair.
They came to my living room on Tuesdays, some of them in their slippers. So,

Movement number three. Seated marching. Back straight, hands on the seat of the chair
or on your knees if that is easier. Now pick up one foot,
set it down, pick up the other, set it down. Like a marching soldier
the knee a little, not high. Little is fine. Why marching in a chair?
Because it wakes the hip. The hip is a big joint and it likes to
be used. When you lift the knee, the front of the hip opens and the
thigh does the work and the circulation. The blood moves down to the feet
while waiting for the rice to finish cooking. She said, march while the
rice cooks and the rice will not wait for you. She marched 20 steps
in the kitchen beside the pot. 20 steps, count out loud.
Movement number 4. Ankle circles. Sit up straight. Lift one foot just
a little off the floor. Now draw a circle with the toes.
Like you are drawing a circle on a table with a pencil, and the pencil is your big
toe. Ten circles one way, ten circles the other way.
Then the other foot. Same, gentle, never fast.
Why the ankle? Because the ankle is the door to the ground.
Every step you take starts at the ankle. If it is stiff, the
walk is short and careful. Little circles open that door again.
had told her to. She just felt they were tight. She did them every

On the bad days, I did them with her. One foot each,
sitting side by side on that chair. Then the other foot. Ten circles.
Breathe slowly while you draw. And when you finish, rest

Movement number 5. Deep breathing with a slow arm lift. Sitting
and lift the arms out to the sides and up to the ceiling. At the top,
hold for one slow breath. Then lower the arms as you breathe out, five
times, only five, and each one slower than the last.
Why breathing? Because the body is not only the legs.
When we breathe slowly, the whole body slows down with us. And a slow breath before
you stand up makes the standing easier. It is like a small pause before
the music. My grandmother finished this way every morning for 60 years.
Arms up, breathe in, arms down, breathe out.
Then she would say, now the day can start. And she stood up and she went out.
